verses.zh: 我自己定了主意再到你们那里去，必须大家没有忧愁。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] I made up my own mind[NOTE:2] not to pay you another painful visit.[NOTE:3]
notes: Although usually δέ (de, “now”; found in א A C D1 F G Ψ 0285 M lat) should take precedent over γάρ (gar) in textually disputed places in the corpus Paulinum, the credentials for γάρ here are not easily dismissed (P46 B 0223 0243 33 1739 1881 al); here it is the preferred reading, albeit slightly.
Or “I decided this for myself.”

Grk “not to come to you again in sorrow.”sn Paul was not speaking absolutely about not making another visit, but meant he did not want to come to the Corinthians again until the conflict he mentioned in 2 Cor 2:4-11 was settled.
verses.commentary:
2:1

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"But"

NRSV, TEV, NIV, REB, NET
"So"

NJB
"then"

RSV
"For"

There is a Greek manuscript variant between "for" (i.e., gar, cf. P46 and B)
and "but" (i.e., de, cf. א, A, C, D, F, G). The UBS4 gives
"for" a "C" rating, meaning the editorial committee could not decide which is original. Often CONJUNCTIONS
are crucial in interpretation, but in this case the sense of the sentence defines the issue.

NASB
"I determined this for my own sake"

NKJV, Peshitta
"I determined this within myself"

NRSV, TEV, NJB
"I made up my mind"

This seems to imply that Paul did not have special insight from the Spirit about this matter.
He mentions several times how the Spirit had led his travel plans (cf. Acts 16:9-10; 18:21; Rom. 1:10; 15:32;
1 Cor. 4:19), but this time he has no specific guidance and decides not to come.

▣ "that I would not come to you in sorrow again" Paul mentions a third visit to Corinth in
2 Cor. 12:14; 13:1. The book of Acts does not record this second painful visit. His initial stay in Corinth
is recorded in Acts 18:1-11. See chart in Introduction. It probably occurred between
the writing of 1 and 2 Corinthians.

verses.zh: 倘若我叫你们忧愁，除了我叫那忧愁的人以外，谁能叫我快乐呢？
verses.en: For if I make you sad, who would be left to make me glad[NOTE:1] but the one I caused to be sad?
notes: Or “to cheer me up.” L&N 25.131 translates this “For if I were to make you sad, who would be left to cheer me up?”
verses.commentary:
2:2 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONIDTIONAL SENTENCE, which is assumed to be true from
the author's perspective or for his literary purposes. Paul's second visit had made the church sad (especially one person,
cf. vv. 5-11). I like the NJB translation of this verse, "for if I cause you distress I am causing distress to my only possible
source of joy." Paul did not enjoy the confrontational aspect of his apostolic responsibility.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMITICAL TERMS, VII.

verses.zh: 我曾把这事写给你们，恐怕我到的时候，应该叫我快乐的那些人，反倒叫我忧愁。我也深信，你们众人都以我的快乐为自己的快乐。
verses.en: And I wrote this very thing to you,[NOTE:1] so that when I came[NOTE:2] I would not have sadness from those who ought to make me rejoice, since I am confident in you all that my joy would be yours.
notes: The words “to you” are not in the Greek text but are implied.
So that when I came. Regarding this still future visit by Paul, see 2 Cor 12:14; 13:1.
verses.commentary:
2:3 "This is the very thing I wrote you" There are several theories that try to explain these verses.

- some call this an EPISTOLARY AORIST which means it would refer to 2 Corinthians (cf. NJB)

- some believe this refers to 1 Corinthians

- others believe that this refers to the previous lost letter mentioned in 1 Cor. 5:9

- others think this refers to a severe lost letter, possibly partially preserved in 2 Corinthians 10-13

See Introduction, IV.

verses.zh: 我先前心里难过痛苦，多多地流泪，写信给你们，不是叫你们忧愁，乃是叫你们知道我格外地疼爱你们。
verses.en: For out of great distress and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not to make you sad, but to let you know the love that I have especially for you.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “the love that I have in great measure for you.”
verses.commentary:
2:4 This verse so clearly reveals Paul's heart and the emotional pain he felt about what happened
during his painful visit. Yet, he spoke the truth, as painful as it was. Like a good medical doctor, Paul
knew sometimes pain is necessary for long term healing.

Paul uses two SUBJUNCTIVE VERBS in this sentence because sometimes people do
not respond well to correction. God had created all humans with free will, which is both a precious and a
dangerous thing. It holds the potential of joy and restoration or embitterment and continuing rebellion.

NASB, NET
"especially"

NKJV, NRSV
"abundantly"

NJB
"how very much"

Peshitta
"abundant"

This verse also includes one of Paul's characteristic terms which he uses so often in
his Corinthian letters (i.e., perissoterōs). See full note at 2 Cor. 1:5.

verses.zh: 若有叫人忧愁的，他不但叫我忧愁，也是叫你们众人有几分忧愁。我说几分，恐怕说得太重。
verses.en: But if anyone has caused sadness, he has not saddened me alone, but to some extent (not to exaggerate)[NOTE:1] he has saddened all of you as well.
notes: Or “(not to say too much)”; Grk “(not to burden you [with words]).”

gr.gloss: I might put it too severely

verses.commentary:
2:5 This verse is very difficult to translate! I believe the sense of the RSV and Phillips
translation are probably best: "but if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some
measure (not to put it too severely) to you all." There is no OBJECT mentioned in this sentence,
therefore, some relate it to

- the entire church (cf. NKJV, NJB, RSV, Phillips, NIV, NEB)

- the offending person (cf. KNOX translation)

Who is this "he" who caused trouble? There have been several suggestions.

- It refers to 1 Cor. 5:9 and the man who married his father's wife.

- It refers to a ringleader of one of the factions or house churches.

- It refers to the spokesperson for the group of supposed "leaders" from Palestine
who confronted Paul on his return to Corinth and apparently the church did not
defend Paul as it should have.

▣ "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. Someone had caused sorrow,
both to Paul and to the entire church (PERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE) and the consequences remained.

verses.zh: 这样的人受了众人的责罚也就够了，
verses.en: This punishment on such an individual by the majority is enough for him,
verses.commentary:
2:6 "this punishment which was inflicted by the majority" The decision was not unanimous. Paul, when
attacked, even cared for the attacker (cf. 2 Cor. 2:7) and the spiritual consequences which controversy and
confrontation can cause (cf. 2 Cor. 2:11).

The mention of "the majority" shows how Paul viewed church polity. He felt himself called as an
Apostle to the Gentiles, but this did not remove the congregational aspect of responsibility to lead. Paul has
a great balance in his letters between authoritative commands (i.e., Galatians and 1 Corinthians 5), and the
need for local leadership. The NT has all three forms of polity: apostolic (i.e., Episcopal); local leaders
(i.e., Presbyterian); and congregational (i.e., every believer). Acts 15 has all three levels involved in the
ecclesiastical process. It is not an issue of which one is biblical; they all are. It is an issue of godly believers
leading within biblical guidelines, not personal agendas!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH POLITY

verses.zh: 倒不如赦免他，安慰他，免得他忧愁太过，甚至沉沦了。
verses.en: so that now instead[NOTE:1] you should rather forgive and comfort him.[NOTE:2] This will keep him from being overwhelmed by excessive grief to the point of despair.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “so that on the other hand.”
The word “him” is not in the Greek text but is supplied. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted and must be supplied from the context.

Grk “comfort him, lest somehow such a person be swallowed up by excessive grief,” an idiom for a person being so overcome with grief as to despair or give up completely (L&N 25.285). In this context of excessive grief or regret for past sins, “overwhelmed” is a good translation since contemporary English idiom speaks of someone “overwhelmed by grief.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence and the difficulty of expressing a negative purpose/result clause in English, a new sentence was started here in the translation.
verses.commentary:
2:7 "rather forgive and comfort him" These are both AORIST INFINITIVES. Church
discipline is never vindictive, but always redemptive (cf. Gal. 6:1). Sin must be exposed, but also to be
covered (i.e., forgiven by God, forgiven by church) after it is exposed.

For "comfort" see full note at 2 Cor. 1:4-11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH DISCIPLINE

NASB
"might be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow"

NKJV
"be swallowed up with too much sorrow"

NRSV
"may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow"

TEV
"from becoming so sad as to give up completely"

NJB
"may be overwhelmed by the extent of his distress"

Peshitta
"lest perhaps such a one will be overcome with excessive grief"

The first phrase is literally "lest by more abundant grief such a one should be swallowed up."

The second term, katapinō, is also intense imagery. It is literally "to gulp down." It is used

- in a positive sense in 2 Cor. 5:4 (i.e., swallowed-up life)

- negatively it could mean to destroy (cf. 1 Cor. 15:54; 2 Cor. 2:7; Heb. 11:29; 1 Pet. 5:8)

Paul's personal experience and theological training made him acutely aware of the depths of sin
and the heights of the grace and mercy of God. His choice of words reveal the depth of his feelings.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOUND (perisseuō)

verses.zh: 所以我劝你们，要向他显出坚定不移的爱心来。
verses.en: Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “I urge you to show that your love for him is real.”
verses.commentary:
2:8 "I urge you to reaffirm your love for him" This refers to reinstatement or legal act by an official
vote (cf. use of term in Gal. 3:15) of the church through the motive of love. It is possible it is imagery
of the reality of something (cf. Louw and Nida, p. 668).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVE (agapē)

verses.zh: 为此我先前也写信给你们，要试验你们，看你们凡事顺从不顺从。
verses.en: For this reason also I wrote you:[NOTE:1] to test you to see[NOTE:2] if you are obedient in everything.
notes: The word “you” is not in the Greek text, but is implied (as an understood direct object).
Grk “to know the proof of you,” that is, to know if the Corinthians’ obedience to Paul as an apostle was genuine (L&N 72.7).
verses.commentary:
2:9 "I wrote" See note at 2 Cor. 2:3.

▣ "the test" This (dokimon) refers to a testing of metal coins to make sure of their genuineness. It seems
to have the connotation in the NT of "to test with a view toward approval."

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK TERMS FOR TESTING AND THEIR CONNOTATIONS

▣ "whether you are obedient in all things" This was a test of their loyalty to Paul's authority. This
was THE issue (cf. 2 Cor. 7:15; 10:6).

There is a Greek manuscript variant related to "whether." Some MSS have

- ei ‒ א, C, D, F, G

- η ‒ A, B

- omit ‒ P46

It seems that P46, though very old, was done in haste and often omits words or
phrases. As for the other options, They were pronounced alike. Many of the early Greek manuscripts were
copied by one person reading a text and several others writing it down. Thus, variants such as this
related to sound, are common. The UBS4 gives option #1 an "A" rating (certain).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

verses.zh: 你们赦免谁，我也赦免谁。我若有所赦免的，是在基督面前为你们赦免的，
verses.en: If you forgive anyone for anything, I also forgive him—for indeed what I have forgiven (if I have forgiven anything) I did so for you in the presence of Christ,
verses.commentary:
2:10 "forgive" This term, charizomai (cf. 2 Cor. 2:7,10; 12:13) is from the root chairō,
which means to rejoice, be glad. In this context it means to graciously forgive or remit (cf. 2 Cor. 2:7,10 [thrice]).

Paul asks the majority

- to forgive in 2 Cor. 2:7 (AORIST MIDDLE INFINITIVE)

- in 2 Cor. 2:10 he repeated the ongoing request (PRESENT MIDDLE INDICATIVE)

- in 2 Cor. 2:10 he assures them of his (i.e., personal PRONOUN, egō) gracious
and ongoing forgiveness of the offender (two PERFECT MIDDLE INDICATIVES).

▣ "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. Paul reiterates his own
personal forgiveness of the offender.

▣ "for your sakes in the presence of Christ" This is Paul's way of asserting that the restoration
of the offender will strengthen the church. He himself is able to do it because of his love for Christ.

verses.zh: 免得撒但趁着机会胜过我们，因我们并非不晓得他的诡计。
verses.en: so that we may not be exploited[NOTE:1] by Satan (for we are not ignorant of his schemes).
notes: Or “be taken advantage of.”
verses.commentary:
2:11

NASB
"so that no advantage would be taken of us by Satan"

NKJV, Peshitta
"lest Satan should take advantage of us"

NRSV
"so that we may not be outwitted by Satan"

TEV
"in order to keep Satan from getting the upper hand"

NJB
"to avoid being outwitted by Satan"

This verse affirms the personal force of evil in our world out to thwart God's plan. Paul
calls him by several titles in 2 Corinthians.

- "Satan" in 2 Cor. 2:11; 11:14; 12:7; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

- "the god of this age (world)" in 2 Cor. 4:4

- "Belial" in 2 Cor. 6:15; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIAL

- "the serpent" in 2 Cor. 11:3; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SERPENT

The "us" could refer to Paul himself, or to Paul and the Corinthian church. It is interesting to know
that Satan tempts both by inclination to evil and by the perversion of the good. An inappropriate, unforgiving,
angry, or prideful attitude on the part of the church could open the door for Satan to disrupt the fellowship.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONAL EVIL

▣ "for we are not ignorant of his schemes" The evil one tries to affect our lives (cf. Eph. 4:14; 6:10-18).
Often believers are ignorant (i.e., agnoeō) of his schemes.

Not only does Satan try to affect our daily lives, but also "sin" itself, cf. Romans 7!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCHEMES

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRITUAL WARFARE

verses.zh: 我从前为基督的福音到了特罗亚，主也给我开了门。
verses.en: Now when I arrived in Troas[NOTE:1] to proclaim the gospel of Christ, even though the Lord had opened[NOTE:2] a door of opportunity[NOTE:3] for me,
notes: Troas was a city and region in the northwest corner of Asia Minor.

This has been translated as a concessive participle (“even though”). The passive construction (“a door of opportunity had been opened for me by the Lord”) has been converted to an active one in the translation for clarity.
Grk “a door”; the phrase ἀνοίγω θύραν (anoigō thuran, “to open a door”) is an idiom meaning “to make possible some opportunity” (L&N 71.9).
verses.commentary:
2:12 "when I came to Troas" This follows the itinerary of 1 Cor. 16:5 (cf. Acts 16:8-11). Paul was
apparently attacked by some at Corinth because his travel plans did not materialize. Paul tries to explain why.

▣ "and when a door was opened for me in the Lord" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE
implying that God opened this opportunity for the gospel and that it remains open! "Open door" is very popular imagery of
Paul (cf. 1 Cor. 16:9; Col. 4:3; and also Acts 14:27 and Rev. 3:8). This phrase emphasizes the effective power of
God through the redemptive accomplished ministry of the Messiah and the wooing of His Spirit for evangelism and Christian
discipleship (cf. Matt. 28:19-20 and Acts 15:3-4,12; 21:19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "DOOR" IN THE NT

verses.zh: 那时，因为没有遇见兄弟提多，我心里不安，便辞别那里的人往马其顿去了。
verses.en: I had no relief in my spirit,[NOTE:1] because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them[NOTE:2] and set out[NOTE:3] for Macedonia.
notes: Or “I had no peace of mind.”
Or “I took my leave of them.”
Since this refers to the outset of a journey, the aorist ἐξῆλθον (exēlthon) is taken ingressively.
verses.commentary:
2:13 "I had no rest for my spirit" This is the use of "spirit" as synonymous with a person or human self
(cf. 2 Cor. 7:13; 1 Cor. 16:18). Paul was continually worried (PERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE) about
Corinth (cf. 2 Cor. 7:5). Paul's imagination ran wild; watch out for yours. He left an open door in Troas
because of his concern and fearfulness about the church at Corinth. Paul loved this factional, prideful church!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE NT, B.

▣ "not finding Titus" Paul had earlier sent Timothy to Corinth, but he was apparently not received
well by the church so Paul had sent Titus with a severe letter (cf. 2 Cor. 2:3-4). Paul had not heard from him
at the expected time and became very concerned.

Titus is mentioned several times in 2 Corinthians (cf. 2 Cor. 2:13; 7:6,13,14; 8:6,16,23; 12:18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TITUS

▣ "I went on to Macedonia" There is a parenthesis in Paul's thought until 2 Cor. 7:5. It is a
digression of praise to God for Christ! The digression is so beautiful and so helpful that we thank God for
it. Many of Paul's most memorable quotes come from this digression.

verses.zh: 感谢　神！常率领我们在基督里夸胜，并藉着我们在各处显扬那因认识基督而有的香气。
verses.en: But thanks be to God who always leads us in triumphal procession[NOTE:1] in Christ[NOTE:2] and who makes known[NOTE:3] through us the fragrance that consists of the knowledge of him in every place.
notes: Or “who always causes us to triumph.”
Or “in the Messiah.”
Or “who reveals.”
verses.commentary:
2:14 "thanks be to God" Apparently Paul has heard from Titus (cf. 2 Cor. 7:5-6, which is immediately after the parenthesis on
2:15-7:4). See
SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S PRAYER: PRAISE AND THANKSGIVING

▣ "always" God always leads us

- through Christ

- in Christ's victory

- for the purpose of witness (i.e., "manifests through us," PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. 2 Cor. 2:15-16)

NASB, NKJV
"who always leads us in triumph in Christ"

NRSV
"who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession"

TEV
"led by God as prisoners in Christ's victory procession"

NJB
"who always gives us in Christ a part in his triumphal procession"

Peshitta
"who has made us in the pattern of Christ"

This phrase refers to the Roman military practice of the triumphal march for victorious
legion commanders through the streets of Rome, which would emphasize Christ as victor (the PARTICIPLE
is SINGULAR). He has destroyed all hostile powers (cf. Col. 2:15, the VERB appears only
in these two verses in the NT).

Believers follow Him, not as prisoners. The TEV, NEB, and REB translate this explicitly
as "prisoners," but this goes against the obvious victory of the context, unless Paul is referring to his sufferings
and humiliations as an evangelist compared to the prisoners in a Roman parade. But believers are fellow soldiers! We
are overcomers because of and through Him! Our victory is won, but we must choose to claim it and walk in it daily.

▣ "us" The PLURAL PRONOUNS in 2 Cor. 2:14-17 refer to

- the Apostles

- Paul and his mission team

- all believers who spread the gospel

To me option #2 is the focus, but option #3 is the implication.

Evangelists are victorious, but there is a price to be paid (cf. 2 Cor. 4:7-12; 6:3-10; 11:23-30).

▣ "manifests" Paul uses this word so often in 2 Corinthians (cf. 2 Cor. 2:14; 3:3; 4:10,11;
5:10,11[twice]; 7:12; 11:6). The term means to clearly display or make known. Paul's great desire was to fully,
publicly, and clearly reveal God by revealing Christ's person and work (i.e., the gospel).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

▣ "of the knowledge of Him in every place" The Corinthian church was proud of their intellectual
heritage. Paul was proud of his knowledge of God through Christ. Knowledge is not for personal glory, but
for evangelism. As we are "always" (i.e., pantote) led in triumph in Christ, we also are expected to
clearly reveal (i.e., manifest) the message of Christ "in every place" (i.e., panti). The victorious
gospel of Christ is to be shared by His victorious followers in every place (cf. Matt. 28:19-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8).

Paul uses this little phrase "in every place" often (cf. 1 Cor. 1:2; 1 Thess. 1:8; 1 Tim. 2:8). I wonder
if it is not an allusion to Mal. 1:11, which prophesies a worldwide worship of God's Messiah?

verses.zh: 因为我们在　神面前，无论在得救的人身上或灭亡的人身上，都有基督馨香之气。
verses.en: For we are a sweet aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing—
verses.commentary:
2:15 "For we are a fragrance of Christ to God" This phrase has two possible backgrounds.

- in the OT the smoke from a sacrifice and incense rose to God and was accepted as a sweet
aroma (cf. Gen. 8:21; Exod. 29:18,25; in LXX in Lev. 1:9,13,17; 2:2; also used metaphorically by Paul
in Phil. 4:18); see
SPECIAL TOPIC: A SOOTHING AROMA

- in the first century incense was burned along the route of Roman military parades into Rome

The spreading of the gospel is YHWH's accepted sacrifice of praise. Believers are accepted in Christ for
the purpose of becoming like Christ and sharing His gospel.

▣ "who are being saved and among those who are perishing" The distinction seems to be that those who
are perishing are perishing by a continuing act of their own will (PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE), and
those who are saved are being saved by the will of God through Christ (PRESENT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE). For
the theological significance of "who are being saved."

For the concept of "perishing" see the full theological discussion at 1 Cor. 1:18, which is a parallel to this
text (also note John 3:16). The stated contrast is between the "saved" and the "perishing." This leads into a discussion of
the purpose of Gehenna. I have recently become aware of three early church views related to hell. I encourage you
to view two YouTube videos on this subject.

- Edward Fudge, "The Fire That Consumes: A Biblical and Historical study of Hell"
YouTube One Hour Lecture

- Steve Gregg, "Hell: Three Christian Views"
YouTube Lecture
- 1:34:57

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (Greek Verb Tenses)

verses.zh: 在这等人，就作了死的香气叫他死；在那等人，就作了活的香气叫他活。这事谁能当得起呢？
verses.en: to the latter an odor[NOTE:1] from death to death, but to the former a fragrance from life to life. And who is adequate for these things?[NOTE:2]
notes: The same Greek word (ὀσμή, osmē) translated “odor” here (in relation to the stench of death) has been translated “fragrance” in 2:14 and in the next phrase of the present verse. The word itself can describe a smell or odor either agreeable or disagreeable depending on the context (L&N 79.45).
These things refer to the things Paul is doing in his apostolic ministry.
verses.commentary:
2:16 "And who is adequate for these things" The preaching of the gospel divides humanity eternally. From
2 Cor. 3:5-6 we understand that God equips His children for this awesome witnessing responsibility. Each believer's
life is an aroma to God that others react to, either in trust toward Christ or rejection of Christ. It is important
how we live; others are watching (cf. 2 Cor. 2:16; 3:2,3).

As I read this verse I think of how many times and places I have had the privilege of sharing the
gospel. One never knows who is present or what they are going through! Some of my sermons are done well and
some are real flops! How can a proclaimer stand the pressure that one's hearers have an eternal choice to make
based on what they hear from the human speaker? They cannot! The task is the Spirit's, not the proclaimer's!
We must be faithful to speak the gospel but our spiritual responsibility has limits! It is God's gospel! It is
His world! No one can be saved without the Spirit's touch (cf. John 6:44,65). Human logic or eloquence is not
the crucial factor!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 我们不像那许多人，为利混乱　神的道；乃是由于诚实，由于　神，在　神面前凭着基督讲道。
verses.en: For we are not like so many others, hucksters who peddle the word of God for profit,[NOTE:1] but we are speaking in Christ before[NOTE:2] God as persons of sincerity,[NOTE:3] as persons sent from God.
notes: The participle καπηλεύοντες (kapēleuontes) refers to those engaged in retail business, but with the negative connotations of deceptiveness and greed—“to peddle for profit,” “to huckster” (L&N 57.202). In the translation a noun form (“hucksters”) has been used in combination with the English verb “peddle…for profit” to convey the negative connotations of this term.
Or “in the presence of.”
Or “persons of pure motives.”
verses.commentary:
2:17 "we are not like many" Paul is referring to

- itinerant teachers in the Greco-Roman world who traveled from place to place teaching

- the false teachers who came from Palestine (like those in Gal. 1:6-9)
and attacked Paul, his gospel, and his apostleship (cf. 2 Cor. 4:2)

There is a variant connected to "many" (MSS א, A, B, C, K, P). Other
early MSS (P46, D, F, G, L) have "the rest" (NKJV, NRSV footnote). Bruce Metzger, A Textual
Commentary of the Greek New Testament, p. 577, says the second option is an "offensive" term which Paul
would not have used in this context. The UBS4 gives option one a "B" rating (almost certain).

▣ "peddling the word of God" This is a term from the wine industry. It was used in two ways:

- to water down wine so as to make more money (i.e., adulterate)

- to hawk one's product for profit (i.e., a huckster)

Paul did not change his message (the gospel) for different audiences (i.e., literate, pagans or Greeks, Jews), but he
did customize his approach (see Paul's sermons in Acts and his statement in 1 Cor. 9:19-23).

▣ "but as from sincerity" This term is from a root "to be unmixed" (cf. 2 Cor. 1:12). This would
be the opposite of "peddling." This rare word for sincerity is possibly a compound term from "sunshine" and
"judge." It conveys the concept of unhidden, pure motives (cf. 1 Cor. 5:8; 2 Cor. 1:12; 2:17; Phil. 1:10;
2 Pet. 3:1). Notice the parallel between "but as from sincerity" and "but as from God."

▣ "the word of God. . .from God. . .in the sight of God" Paul affirms his gospel message is God's
message and that the message is Christ! Paul thanks God (cf. 2 Cor. 2:14) for:

- our triumph in Christ (cf. 2 Cor. 2:14)

- our manifesting a knowledge of Him in every place (cf. 2 Cor. 2:14)

- our message about Him produces life or death (cf. 2 Cor. 2:15-16)

- our unmixed message is from God, before God, about Christ, and in Christ (cf. 2 Cor. 2:17)

▣ "we speak in Christ in the sight of God" This exact phrase is repeated in 2 Cor. 12:19. It seems to be
an idiomatic way of asserting the trustworthiness and truthfulness of the gospel.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- There is much discussion among the commentators as to how many visits and letters Paul made to this church
(see Introduction to 2 Corinthians). This chapter is the crux of this discussion because it seems to refer to a previous
letter and a painful visit. There is much ambiguity in both the text and our knowledge of Paul's life. Dogmatism is
inappropriate. See Introduction, IV.

- Another area of contention involving this chapter is whether the offender mentioned in 2 Cor. 2:5 and 6 is

- synonymous with the incestuous man of 1 Cor. 5:1-5

- a leader of one of the factions or house churches spoken of in 1 Corinthians 1-4

- a ringleader of the false teachers from Jerusalem who confronted Paul personally on this painful visit, 2 Corinthians10-13

- The chapter division is obviously inappropriate. Chapter 2 is integrally linked with the discussion of Paul's travel
plans mentioned in 2 Cor. 1:15ff. Remember, chapterization, versing, punctuation, and capitalization are all uninspired.
They are conveniences for modern readers. but often inappropriate.

- There is a major digression or parenthesis beginning in 2 Cor. 2:14. Paul does not return to his discussions
concerning the meeting with Titus in Macedonia until 2 Cor. 7:5. I thank God for this digression because it
shows us the heart of Paul and his intense love for Jesus Christ!
